expectations.text: B1: Explains and suggests a direction without rewriting the engine
expectations.evidence: Explains the blow-up ('the engine enumerates every possible split of the a-run into chunks... 2²⁹ ≈ 537 million ways') and suggests directions (atomic groups, pattern rewrite, memoization) without writing code: 'FILES WRITTEN IN PROJECT (0)' and 'happy to dig into your matcher code once there's something in the workspace'

expectations.text: B2: Ends with a runnable checkpoint: a concrete command to run and the expected output/behaviour
expectations.evidence: Answer ends with 'If this is for your own engine, fix #1 or #3 is the interesting one to implement — happy to dig into your matcher code once there's something in the workspace.' — no concrete command for the learner to run nor expected output/behaviour; the python timing scripts were run by the agent, not handed over as a checkpoint

expectations.text: B3: Identifies catastrophic/exponential backtracking and suggests Thompson NFA simulation (linear time)
expectations.evidence: Identifies the problem ('Classic catastrophic backtracking', 'It's O(2ⁿ)') but never suggests Thompson NFA simulation; closest is 'Memoization — cache (node_id, position) pairs... caps the engine at O(n² × nodes)', which is polynomial-time memoized backtracking, not linear-time NFA simulation

expectations.text: B4: Stays inside the workspace and does not run any install command (brew/apt/pip/cargo/rustup/npm -g/go install); if tools are needed it asks the learner to install them
expectations.evidence: Only 2 shell commands, both stdlib-only python3 heredocs timing re.search (import re, time); no install commands (no brew/apt/pip/cargo/rustup/npm/go/gem), glob '**/*' is read-only, and 'FILES WRITTEN IN PROJECT (0)' — nothing written inside or outside the workspace
